correctness.rationale: The theorem is a finite exhaustive classification. Removing consecutive duplicates preserves permutation subsequences; first-occurrence normalization uniquely represents each \(S_5\) orbit. For any t-prefix pattern its earliest occurrence precedes \(L-m_{5-t}\), proved using the complementary suffix. Exact smaller minimum lengths 1,3,7,12 are independently enumerated. Two structurally different enumerators, one using greedy states on 120 permutations and the other explicit distinct-letter-subsequence bitsets, independently give 0 candidates at length 18 and the same 128 canonical length-19 words; Python checks each against all 120 permutations, sorted multiplicities and the reversal partition. The entire claimed finite domain and all pruning steps are accounted for; no nonstandard unproved infinite lemma is used.

evidence: Newey 1973, Section 9 (printed page 12): his construction yields 128 equivalence classes for five symbols and explicitly says they may or may not be all; the very same alphabet-relabeling equivalence is defined on printed page 1.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: This claim uses precisely Newey’s complete-word notion and his relabeling equivalence, not a renamed problem. His 128 examples imply a lower bound, not a global upper bound: his own wording says exhaustion was unresolved. The proof here supplies that missing upper bound. The reversal classification is a consequence of the now-complete list, not a claim to have invented reversal symmetry.

originality.rationale: Newey (1973) constructed 128 distinct five-symbol optimum classes but wrote explicitly that they may or may not be all. The new exhaustive upper bound shows there are no others and so answers the precise historical unresolved equality-case question. The minimum length, construction family and four-symbol classification are credited as prior. Relevant primary texts and database entries were compared by implications rather than terminology; possible later unindexed census remains a priority risk.
residual_risks: Unindexed or inaccessible later census could have established the same global upper bound before this classification.

value.rationale: Exactly counting all shortest complete words is a natural extremal classification and resolves Newey’s explicit 1973 may-or-may-not-be-exhaustive 128-class question. The result supplies a complete optimal-design list, a rigidity statement (all optimal normalized words begin with a full permutation), and symmetry classification (72 reversal orbits), not an arbitrary size slice or re-enumeration of a settled optimum length. The exact finite fact is useful independently of any general formula for larger alphabets.
